claim: Confidence quality has three separate parts: bias (level), sensitivity (separating right from wrong) and efficiency (sensitivity relative to task accuracy). One calibration number mixes them.
agent_test: Score the agent on ECE, type-2 AUROC and an accuracy-adjusted score separately on one item set at equal tokens; report all three.

claim: Correlation scores such as gamma and phi are contaminated by response bias and should not be used to grade confidence.
agent_test: Compare gamma with AUROC2 on the agent runs while shifting its answer threshold; gamma should move, AUROC2 should not. Rests on one review citing the original studies, which were not opened.

claim: Type-2 AUROC is bias-free and needs no Gaussian assumption, but it rises with task accuracy, so it cannot compare across difficulty levels.
agent_test: Plot AUROC2 against accuracy over item-difficulty bins for the agent; expect a positive slope.

claim: No current metacognitive measure is independent of type-1 performance. M-ratio falls with d' in regular and hierarchical fits (hierarchical beta -0.19 +/- 0.05); log M-ratio removes the hierarchical dependence (beta 0.01 +/- 0.02) but a pooled rank correlation of -0.073 remains. Main analyses use 1757 of 6912 subjects (at least 400 trials, d' above 0.5).
agent_test: Check the dependence of the agent efficiency score on accuracy across several difficulty strata before comparing arms.

claim: M-ratio needs about 400 or more trials per subject for acceptable test-retest reliability; at fewer trials it gives extreme or negative values (2.4% negative, 4% above 1.5 overall; 4% and 10% under 200 trials).
agent_test: Agent trials are cheap: use at least 400 items per arm or hierarchical or log M-ratio, and bootstrap the score.

claim: In LLMs, sample agreement predicts failure better than a single verbalized confidence, mainly on arithmetic. GPT-3.5 GSM8K AUROC 54.8 to 92.7 with 5 samples; the five-dataset average gain is smaller (69.2 to 73.0).
agent_test: At equal tokens compare 1 sample plus verbalized confidence against k samples plus agreement share; score AUROC and ECE on arithmetic, code and free-text sets.

claim: Agreement among samples is a consensus, not truth. In people, confidence follows consistency: positive on consensually correct items, negative on consensually wrong ones (16 tasks; seen by Brewer, Sampaio, Bajsanski, Litvinova and others). In LLMs the same class exists (imitative falsehoods) and the semantic-entropy authors state their method does not address systematic errors. The rate of high-agreement-wrong for current LLMs on open-ended and code tasks is not measured in any source found (see K23).
agent_test: Build items where a wrong answer is the common one (known misconceptions, buggy-but-plausible code) and measure the high-agreement-wrong rate and the sign of the agreement-accuracy slope on that slice; test a cross-check by different framing, tool or test.

claim: Grouping sampled answers by meaning before computing entropy predicts correctness better than counting distinct answers. Original numbers (Farquhar 2024, 30 model-task pairs, 10 generations): AUROC 0.790 vs naive entropy 0.691, P(True) 0.698, embedding regression 0.687. Earlier Kuhn 2023 numbers: CoQA 0.77 vs 0.66, TriviaQA 0.83 vs 0.79. The authors say it does not help on systematic errors.
agent_test: For free-text answers cluster by entailment (a cheap judge call) vs exact match; compare AUROC at equal token budget including the judge cost.

claim: Verbalized confidence from RLHF chat models is overconfident and clusters at 80-100 percent with near-chance failure prediction (GPT-4 mean AUROC 62.7; average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3-class models), yet another study found it better calibrated than token probabilities (ECE cut about 50 percent; ChatGPT TriviaQA 0.140 to 0.050). Studies agree discrimination is modest and disagree on calibration ranking.
agent_test: Elicit verbal confidence, token confidence and agreement for the same items; compare ECE and AUROC for the model in use. Treat verbal confidence as unvalidated until checked.

claim: Low ECE can hide useless confidence: GPT-4 on GSM8K (93.6 percent accuracy) had ECE 0.064 by saying 100 percent always. Calibration without a discrimination score is not enough.
agent_test: Always report AUROC2 or within-question discrimination next to ECE; flag constant-confidence outputs.

claim: Weighting each sampled answer by the model own confidence cuts the samples needed to match plain majority vote by about 40 percent (P(True) 46 percent at budget 10; verbal 1-100 30 percent; verbal binary 10 percent) with accuracy gains of 0.2 to 1.6 points. The P(True) self-check costs about 20 input tokens and 1 output token when the prefix is cached, so the saving survives cost counting there; without prefix caching, re-billing each sample prefix may erase much of it (my reading, not tested). Open-weights models up to 123B, none a reasoning model.
agent_test: Run weighted vs plain majority vote on the agent at equal total tokens including self-check calls; measure with and without prompt caching.

claim: Within one question, the higher-confidence answer is correct only 52 to 62 percent of the time (WQD: 52.2 verbal binary to 62.3 P(True)); confidence ranks questions better than it ranks answers within a question.
agent_test: Measure within-question discrimination for the agent candidate answers before using confidence to choose between them.

claim: Token-level confidence inside a reasoning trace can filter weak traces: sliding-window confidence stops low-confidence traces early. DeepConf-low saved 43.8 to 84.7 percent of tokens (84.7 is the best cell; DeepConf-high 18.8 to 59.0) against 512-trace voting, with a few accuracy drops from overconfident wrong traces. It needs token log-probabilities, so it does not run on a plain chat API. A logprob-free alternative exists for stopping: Adaptive-Consistency stops on agreement among finished samples (average 3.3x fewer samples, 0.04 percent accuracy drop on 2023 models). Agreement among partial traces is untested.
agent_test: If logprobs are available, prune lowest-window-confidence samples at equal total tokens. If not, use an agreement stop rule on finished samples and compare.

claim: About 1000 graded examples with LoRA fine-tuning beat prompting for uncertainty estimates; prompting alone is insufficient. RLHF reward models themselves favour high stated confidence, which makes chat models verbally overconfident.
agent_test: Not applicable to a scaffold-only agent; instead calibrate post hoc with a small held-out set, as in temperature scaling.

claim: A one-parameter post-hoc temperature rescaling fixes calibration of modern vision nets (CIFAR-100 ResNet-110 ECE 16.53 to 1.26 percent; ImageNet ResNet-152 5.48 to 1.86 percent). LLM transfer is shown only by Tian et al.
agent_test: Fit a monotone map from agreement share to accuracy on a held-out set and apply it; compare ECE before and after.

claim: Metacognitive information of LLM token confidence differs 1.98-fold across four 8-9B models and is not reliably predicted by accuracy (rank correlation -0.80 TriviaQA, 0.00 NQ); the author withdrew an earlier stronger claim after a scorer error. After the fix, 18.4 percent of answers the scorer still rejects are correct and this residual varies 2.4-fold between models; the author says generalisation to frontier scale is unknown.
agent_test: When comparing models or arms, do not assume accuracy ranks them on confidence quality; check the scorer against human labels first.

claim: When type-1 sensitivity differs, AUROC2 and M-ratio can give opposite verdicts on LLMs (across tasks AUC2 vs d' Spearman rs 0.9). Prompted-confidence LLM M-ratios of about 0.62 to 0.92 are reported (Servajean: moderate 0.65 to near-optimal 0.90; Dai range second-hand).
agent_test: Use M-ratio (or log) for cross-task comparison and AUROC2 within a task; the Dai range needs the original source.

claim: Metacognitive efficiency correlates across tasks in people (5 of 6 cross-task correlations, N=181), supporting partial domain generality, though settled only with hierarchical models.
agent_test: Test whether agent confidence quality on one task type predicts it on another; if not, calibrate per task type.

claim: Humans over-trust default LLM explanations: user AUC 0.59 to 0.60 against model AUC 0.75 to 0.78; longer explanations raise user confidence without raising discrimination (human AUC 0.54); matching wording to model confidence narrows the gaps. In a pre-registered study (N=404) first-person hedges raised accuracy from 63.9 to 72.8 percent and cut agreement from 80.9 to 74.8; general-perspective hedges were not significant. No study yet uses confidence computed from sample agreement.
agent_test: In the final answer state confidence in a form matched to the agreement score; avoid long justification as a trust cue.

claim: Human confidence is shaped by countable cues such as ease of processing and consensus (Koriat 1997, 2008, 2012). The original Koriat papers were not opened here, so this is analogy only.
agent_test: Do not use as support beyond analogy; validate with the LLM studies above.

claim: LLMs can report and control only a small low-dimensional subset of their activations, so introspective self-report is a weak basis for confidence.
agent_test: Prefer externally countable signals (agreement, tests) over asking the model how sure it is.

claim: In people the consistency-confidence pattern (positive confidence-accuracy on consensually correct items, negative on consensually wrong) holds in at least 16 tasks and was seen by at least four groups beyond Koriat. Exact effect sizes and N for Koriat 2012 were not obtained (paper paywalled; abstracts and a 2025 open review read).
agent_test: Treat agreement-confidence as valid on typical items and untrusted on adversarial or misconception items; report both slices.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: No source measures how often high agreement is wrong for current frontier LLMs on open-ended or code tasks, or which cheap check (different framing, tool, test) best breaks it. Closest: TruthfulQA (2021 models) and the voting plateau in Large Language Monkeys.
agent_test: Measure the rate on the agent own item set with a misconception slice; compare framing change, tool call and test execution as breakers.

claim: A calibration map fitted on one task transfers only to tasks of the same kind with similar base rates. For code with GPT-3.5, skill 0.14 to 0.12 between two synthesis tasks, but 0.12 to -1.28 from a repair-style set to synthesis. More than 64 labelled points are needed before skill turns positive.
agent_test: Fit one map per task family on a few hundred labelled items and check base-rate match before reuse.

claim: Verbalized confidence quality depends on the scale. For six models incl. GPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, M-ratio at 0-100 runs 0.62 to 0.92; a 0-20 scale raised it for most models and raising the scale floor lowered it (GPT-5.2 0.92 to 0.69). Three values cover 78 to 92 percent of answers.
agent_test: Do not compare models on a single verbal scale; prefer agreement counts which have a natural fine scale.

claim: Reasoning models are better at verbalized confidence in 32B open models (33 of 36 settings) but API reasoning models are overconfident (above 85 percent even when wrong) and more so with more reasoning effort. Neither study compares verbalized with agreement confidence at equal tokens.
agent_test: Run the head-to-head (agreement vs verbalized, equal total tokens, AUROC2 and ECE) on the agent own model and tasks.

claim: A logprob-free agreement stop rule exists: Adaptive-Consistency (Dirichlet model of the lead) cut samples up to 7.9x, average 3.3x, with 0.04 percent accuracy drop over 17 datasets and 3 models (2023).
agent_test: Adopt as the stopping rule when logprobs are missing; recheck on a current model.

claim: Voting plateaus while coverage keeps rising: Llama-3-8B on MATH coverage 82.9 to 98.44 percent from 100 to 10,000 samples, majority vote only 40.50 to 41.41. Where tests exist (code) coverage turns into accuracy (SWE-bench Lite 15.9 to 56 percent). Tests do not vote, so they break false consensus.
agent_test: For code, define agreement by test outputs and let tests, not votes, decide.

claim: Confidence-weighted aggregation amplifies the majority tendency: in human pairs the more confident member beat the better member on consensually correct items but was worse than the worse member on consensually wrong items.
agent_test: Check CISC-style weighting on the consensually wrong slice separately.

claim: Metric choice for grading the agent stays open. AUROC2 is inflated by few confidence levels (two-bin use in Yoon 2025), M-ratio from a single binarised threshold is crude (Dai 2026), and Guggenmos asks about 400 or more trials per arm. A rough budget at 400 items x 10 samples x about 3,000 tokens is about 12 million tokens per arm (my estimate, not from a source).
agent_test: Report AUROC2 with many-level scores plus ECE; use within-question discrimination for the vote-weighting test; use M-ratio only with 400 or more items.
